[b]The daily gambit[/b]

What's it like being an aquanaut? It's equally humorous and terrible. Humans aren't meant to explore the depths of the oceans and lakes. The deeper you go, the stronger the pressure acting on your body, and the more nitrogen and helium starts accumulating into your body's tissues. Blood, fat, nerves, they dissolve into it all. If you resurface all at once, these gasses pop back into bubbles deep within your body. They start tearing you up inside out, and you die.

Regular divers contend with this dilemma all the time. They go into the world beneath the world for an hour, finish their mission, and then ascend again. However, then they stop at a specific point. Decompression starts, and they're forced to just idle in the open seas, waiting patiently as the nitrogen and helium slowly exit their bodies. This takes a while, a very inefficient while. 1 hour of work at 250 feet gives you nearly 5 hours of decompression. Then, the decompression finishes, you ascend, and then after a while you do it all again. All that labor, interspersed between hours of doing absolutely nothing. And if you're going 1,000 feet and deeper? Decompression could take days at a time. 

That isn't a productive way of doing things. And so, aquanauts come into the picture. We cannot fight against the laws of nature and we cannot prevent gas from saturating our bodies at extreme depths. Therefore, why not accept it?

An aquanaut is a bit different from a regular diver. Like them, they go on ships toward their places of work, but these ships are a bit different. On them were hyperbaric chambers; small, liveable spaces pressurized to the exact same pressure as the world below. Here, these aquanauts sit around for a day, breathing in heliox (helium and oxygen) until their bodies were fully saturated. Once done, they enter another, much smaller diving chamber called a "bell" which takes them down to the bottom. The bell's also hyperbaric and keeps the aquanauts saturated the whole way through. Then, the aquanauts do their work, enter the bell, and rise back up to the ship and relax inside their chambers, all without ever having to worry about decompression, when every single component of their dive keeps them pressurized the whole way through.

Oh, and if you're wondering, yes. Heliox causes funny voices. When aquanauts work, they talk with high-pitched voices. And no, we never considered nitrogen as an alternative, because that just makes you high as a kite. Could be fun, if you weren't supposed to be working a thousand feet below the surface of the Qianxun Lakes.

Anyways, after their job's done, we start decompression. The beauty of saturation is that you can't get any more saturated. You can hang at 1 day, 10 days, or 30 days at that pressure, but the time for decompression always stay the same. In the Qianxun Lakes, this usually takes about two weeks. Still long, but at least it's only once at the very end of the mission. Without all these hyperbaric chambers, divers are forced to decompress for those two weeks every single time they finish their work to eat, sleep, take a crap, or log their results.

Of course, the job isn't all that simple. There's a reason why Qianxun pays its aquanauts 60,000 yuan (around C$1,000) for every single day they spend in the water. People have died and will continue to die, and part of the job is to fetch the corpses of the ones that came before you.

Which brings us to the Qianxun Lakes.

Now, it would be surprising enough for you to realize that we only ever do saturation dives at one of the lakes. Lake Qianxun Major, that's the larger, western lake controlled by Kuanlo College. Some research is also conducted at Lake Qianxun Minor, but the place is generally off-limits to most.

Qianxun Major is a violent lake. Its waters are terror. Meanwhile, Qianxun Minor is always tranquil, its surface always a radiant blue in the morning and a beautiful illumination beneath the starlight. And yet, we go to chaos, because at least it seemingly tolerates out presence.

I'll be serious now, but do not go to Qianxun Minor's waters. We've sent dozens of men to their deaths in that lake. Every time, it's the same thing. We saturate the finest aquanauts in Amaralo with inert gasses and send them into the depths. They come up, prepare for decompression, but fall dead. We sent scuba divers to tear through the shallow waters, and they collapse the moment they go to shore. Swimmers too, and animals, and even boats, whose engines seemingly fall apart mere minutes into voyage.

Lake Qianxun Major is different. Even amidst its fury is hospitality. Enter on the great military vessels provisioned by the Qianxun Navy and brave the mist and storms, then descend beneath the torrent and you will find that the lake welcomes you to explore the world beneath the world. You'll be tossed around by an unseen force, the umbilical cord of the bell will dangle ominously, and every second you will doubt if whatever is being studied here will be worth the risk, but then you survive, and you'll realize that the risk there was just a facade.

Oh? You're asking why we bother?

Well, that's a silly question. We do this daily gambit because it's what's been requested of us. Listen carefully friend. Lay your head on your desk and face the lake. You hear it too, don't you? She's out there, waiting.

[quote=the_crystalline_empire;60296363][b]Vive-L'empereur[/b]
Emperor Erjk Drs walked slowly down the aisle of the St. Joseph Orthodox Church in the principality of Sheba, his robes red and gold, patterns of flora and fauna decorating them. In his left hand he held a gold staff, tipped with a crystal eagle, in his right, a small crystal, pearl, and sapphire orb model of Erene. Around him the choirs of the Ismyr Mens Choir sang ancient hymns in Arabic, and before him, the patriarch of Thýven, standing before the iconostasis, berobed in far more grandeur than the emperor before him.

Emperor Erjk Drs, began the patriarch, Do you understand the crown which you are to take, he asked.

I do, replied the emperor, kneeling, and bowing his antlered head before the primarch of christianity. 

The patriarch would nod, before intoning the great litany over the assembled church and the Emperor. As the service continued the sun shone brightly through the windows of the dome of the cathedral, casting a sacred glow upon the Emperor and the patriarch, for those assembled in the crowd, it was taken as a divine sign that the Emperor was truly chosen by God.

Finally as the hymns and service began to reach its peak, a new Imperial crown was brought forward, incense was cast over it, and then the Emperor, kneeling upon a cushion, would be crowned with it. The crown was a bulky figure upon the Emperors head, his antlers framing it like a painting, its jewels and gold shining in the candlelight of the cathedral. 

Following the crowning, the Emperor would be permitted to rise, doing so a little unsteadily, and turning to the crowd he would be declared, Ἰδοὺ, ὁ Θεόδοτος Αὐτοκράτωρ, Ἐρζκ Δρῷς, Αὐτοκράτωρ τῆς Ἐλεσυρ-Σαμάτ, συμβασιλεὺς τῶν Βεσπουρίων, πρίγκιψ τῆς Σαβᾶ, Δούξ τῆς Ἴσμυρ.  (Behold, the God given Emperor, Erjk Drs, Emperor of Elesyr-Shamat, co-emperor of Vespurias, prince of Sheba, Duke of Ismyr). 

The crowd would rise up in cheers as cries of  Long live the gracious Emperor, may his reign be blessed!

Of course for a keen observer of the coronation, one would notice that the title of Elesyr-Shamat had been attributed to the Emperor, a bold move that had been heavily debated in the legislature, and not given full assent by the representatives, however, by this point the matter could not be driven any further, as the Emperor now lay claim to not two, but three continents under his Sacred protection.

[b]Fallout[/b]

EMPEROR OF ELESYR-SHAMAT?! Shouted a voice as the Gøsfodde came into order, news had spread of the recent coronation, which had been done without legislative approval.

How much money was spent? Was it state money? enquired another voice as the various Fondenfoddel gathered in their respective groups on the chamber floor.

What constitutional authority does the Emperor have to do this? enquired yet another from a corner of the room.

Gentlemen, and ladies, please let us calm down, began the Steward of the Royal House, Bjørn Niels.

Calm down?! cried a voice, Are you not aware that the [i]Emperor[/i] or shall we call him [i]autokrator[/i] has declared himself above all authority besides God? 

Bjørn frowned at this outburst replying, The Emperor is within his right to call upon the church to crown him, I see nothing that was done wrong, aside from adding a title to his name, one which I have doubt will be internationally recognised, he replied calmly.

And what does the Emperor of Vespurias say? Has he made a comment? enquired another voice.

No, though I am sure his majesty has made his co-ruler aware of the coronation and ascension, replied Bjørn.

By what constitutional authority does the Emperor have to do this? enquired yet another voice.

Well, given the fact that our constitution is in the process of being re-written, the Emperor has provisional authority to modify his personal office, provided it passes quorum, replied Bjørn, raising his finger as another series of angry mutters began, Which, I shall add, was not completed upon the time of the coronation, and of which negotiations were being made to permit his majesty to do, he continued.

Did the princes approve? enquired the same voice, whom Bjørn had now identified as representative Vinland, a member of the Social Affairs quorum. 

I am not yet privy to the discussions of the princes council, replied Bjørn, However, I am sure they are aware, now is that all? Can we continue to the bill that matters, the one for the expansion of financial resources towards the reconstruction of United Hydronia? he asked, looking around the room for further comment, of which there was none, merely a disgruntled silence, Good, he replied with finality, Let us continue,.

With that the normal session of the chamber began, though an air of disgruntlement continued over the entire process.
